outcome: I can build a short statement and distinguish one thing from several.
explanation: A basic French statement usually names who or what acts, then the action, then what receives it: Lina lit un livre means Lina reads a book. This is called subject–verb–object order. C'est introduces one person or thing; ce sont introduces several. French normally keeps a subject word even when English might leave it out in a short note. An apostrophe joins ce and est into c'est.

outcome: I can choose a subject word for the person or people acting.
explanation: A subject pronoun is a short word replacing a person's name before an action. Je means I; tu means familiar singular you; il and elle mean he and she; on often means we in conversation but takes a singular verb. Nous means we; vous means plural or polite you; ils refers to masculine or mixed groups and elles to an all-feminine group. Je becomes j' before a vowel sound, as in j'aime (I like).

outcome: I can identify a noun's grammatical gender using its article.
explanation: A noun names a person, object or idea. Each French noun has a grammatical gender: masculine or feminine; this is a language category, not a claim about an object's identity. Learn un (a, masculine) or une (a, feminine) with the noun. Some endings help: -tion is usually feminine, but patterns have exceptions. People words sometimes change form, such as étudiant and étudiante (student). Memorize unfamiliar words with their articles.

outcome: I can change a simple noun phrase from one item to several.
explanation: Plural means more than one. Most French nouns add a written s in the plural, although that s is usually silent. Un and une become des; le and la become les. Many nouns ending in -eau add x, as in bateau/bateaux (boat/boats); many ending in -al change to -aux, as in journal/journaux (newspaper/newspapers). Exceptions exist, such as bal/bals (dance/dances). Check unusual spellings rather than adding s blindly.

Regular -ir verbs like finir (to finish) give nous finissons; regular -re verbs like vendre (to sell) give je vends and nous vendons. Not every -ir verb follows finir. Present forms can describe now or a habit.

outcome: I can use essential irregular verbs to describe myself and make a simple request.
explanation: Irregular verbs do not follow one reusable ending pattern. Learn useful forms in messages: je suis (I am), j'ai (I have), je vais (I go), je fais (I do), je viens (I come), je prends (I take), je peux (I can), je veux (I want). Polite requests often use je voudrais (I would like), which you can learn as a whole phrase. French uses avoir for age: j'ai vingt ans means I am twenty. Check the form when the subject changes: nous sommes means we are.
